A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same dual-domain watermark-removal work, renamed from D2RA to DAWN. The methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendix A is included in this comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original watermark-removal experiments across six schemes and two datasets, component ablations, and a 20-image comparison of frequency reconstruction with diffusion regeneration.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and reports additional watermark targets, alignment variants, distortion baselines, regeneration-strength comparisons and failure cases.

M1.justification: The DCT reconstruction, learned frequency mask, L1 objective and diffusion-refinement core remain unchanged. V2 makes perceptual alignment optional and adds neural style-transfer and prompted-harmonization variants to the existing mean–variance correction stage. These extend post-processing without replacing the core algorithm.

E1.justification: MS-COCO and SDP remain the datasets, but watermark coverage expands substantially. Table 2 adds PRC-Watermark, WAM, InvisMark and TrustMark to the original six schemes; Appendix A.6 additionally reports failures against Gaussian Shading and SFWMark. These introduce new watermark-removal scenarios.

E2.justification: The regeneration and imprint-removal baselines remain. Whereas v1 explicitly excludes distortion attacks, v2 evaluates rotation, JPEG compression, cropping, blur, noise and brightness in Appendix A.5/Table 4. This adds a substantial comparator class, despite v2's main text retaining the exclusion statement.

E3.justification: V2 introduces FLOPs-based efficiency comparisons, a regeneration-step sweep with PickScore, and distortion protocols including 75-degree rotation, JPEG quality 25 and cropping at 0.75. The original training/evaluation sample sizes remain unchanged. The newly specified 50 diffusion steps clarify the existing implementation rather than establish a rerun or changed core procedure.

E4.justification: The original component ablations remain, augmented by style-transfer variants for SD-v2 and SDXL. V2 adds regeneration-strength and perceptual-quality analysis, prompted-harmonization failure analysis, and discussion of observed failures on Gaussian Shading and SFWMark. These substantially expand the questions investigated beyond the original component study.

E5.justification: The 20-image Wilcoxon signed-rank test, including p = 9.5 × 10^-7, and image-level detector p-value distributions are retained. V2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals or new statistical uncertainty procedures.

E6.justification: The original six-scheme Table 2 values and original Table 3 ablation rows are unchanged. V2 adds substantial results, including PRC-Watermark success of 67.8%/65.6% on SDP/MS-COCO, style-transfer variants, distortion comparisons and approximately 20% success after prompted harmonization. The original stepwise success curve is replaced by FLOPs/fidelity results; these are new comparisons, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the stated natural-image spectral-decay exponent from alpha approximately 1 to approximately 2. The projection formulation and reconstruction equations otherwise remain equivalent. No theorem or proof is added to establish the newly claimed fundamental tradeoff.

C1.justification: V2 reframes the contribution around a fundamental removal-success–distortion–compute tradeoff, claiming that no current attack achieves all three objectives simultaneously. Compared with v1's emphasis on broadly superior single-pass removal with preserved fidelity, v2 positions DAWN as a low-compute option that accepts greater distortion and foregrounds separate perceptual alignment.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of alignment's role, quality-metric bias, limited control over distortion, and failures on Gaussian Shading/SFWMark. It clarifies that fidelity concerns the watermarked input rather than an unknown clean original. V1's explicit Stable-Diffusion-family generalization caveat is omitted, while Appendix A introduces more specific applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 specifies approximately 50 diffusion steps, gives bit lengths for added schemes, documents Tree-Ring generation through its official implementation, and supplies example harmonization prompts. These improve procedural disclosure without establishing changes to the retained experiments. The original training/evaluation sizes and advertised code URL remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands the watermarking literature discussed, including PRC-Watermark, WAM, InvisMark, TrustMark, Gaussian Shading and SFWMark, and adds references supporting alignment and PickScore. It also revises comparative positioning: DAWN is presented as occupying a favorable compute–quality tradeoff rather than simply outperforming prior attacks.

P1.justification: The paper and method are renamed, and the abstract, introduction and substantial method/results passages are rewritten around computational cost and perceptual tradeoffs. The discussion and conclusion are consolidated, and a structured appendix is introduced. The narrative revision extends well beyond copyediting or added result descriptions.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, transposes and expands Table 2, extends Table 3, and adds Table 4. It replaces the optimization-step success plot with a FLOPs/fidelity radar chart, adds pipeline and regeneration-strength figures, and extends qualitative montages with alignment outputs. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering and relocation.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful coverage, clearer inference-cost disclosure, alignment alternatives and explicit failure cases. However, new central interpretations conflict with their evidence: Appendix A.5 says JPEG/blur fail on semantic watermarks, while Table 4 reports ZODIAC success of 24%/72%; Figure 8 gives regeneration at T=10 a PickScore of 0.884 versus DAWN's 0.03 despite the claim of consistently higher DAWN scores. The benefits coexist with material unresolved contradictions, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
